children.author: compiler-guy
children.text:
Joel Spolsky has a famous post about this:

=-=-=-

A lot of software developers are seduced by the old “80/20” rule. It seems to make a lot of sense: 80% of the people use 20% of the features. So you convince yourself that you only need to implement 20% of the features, and you can still sell 80% as many copies.

Unfortunately, it’s never the same 20%. Everybody uses a different set of features.

https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2001/03/23/strategy-letter-iv...

=-=-=-

Also, there are many image editors _already_ out there of varying levels of power and ease of use. Some open source, some commercial.

And yet Photoshop still rules.

children.text:
I asked precisely that question on their discord. An account of token spends.

Noting that this project is examplary experiment that may demonstrate whether the state of genAI can produce complex software before an explosion of token consumption as the code base grows, or even collapse.

In my experiments, it collapsed, each time I tried. Every 6 months or so I take the challenge. Unless a human intervenes of course. Basically dictating what genAi should do, which becomes more painful than it's worth automating code generation.

People are buzzing about it because it is bold experiment whose outcome may tell us extremely interesting things abut vibe coding with current-generation tools. Most particularly, can you, or can you not build large applications with pure vibe coding? And lots of speculation over whether architectural rot will be better or worse than what humans do. Because human-generated architectures rot out too (Photoshop being an excellent example). I not aware of anyone, so far, who has explored that issue. So far, the grand experiment seems to support "can you not", but the experiment isn't over.

Fascinating stuff. I'm glad somebody else is doing it, and happy that I'm not doing it. Yet. But I will certainly be watching with interest.

I am a professional coder with decades of experience. I use AI regularly, but so far use it very tactically. The big challenge I struggle with at the moment is whether I can trust current-generation models that seem to be increasing in power exponentially at the moment with big tasks.

--- Just to qualify for your arbitrary impressionistic standards on who gets to say what about ArtCraft....

Photoshop: Used it for years. I have a perma-license CS6 copy that runs on Windows only. I sometimes (rarely) boot up my Windows partition when I have particularly complex edits to make. A UI that has rotted out over time. No way I'm paying the extortionate rental prices for current-gen Adobe tools. Their entry-level software seems to be toys, and are not usable for anything serious.

Corel Photopaint: I worked for Corel. I actually really like PhotoPaint, which at least follows a Windows UI convention. Much easier to use than Photoshop; but I have not used it for many years.

Gimp: tried it. Rotted out UI, and an absolutely incomprehensible UI convention (if any). I cannot use it and will not take the time to learn it. On Linux, I very occasionally use Gimp, but I loathe it.

Krita: So much easier to use than Gimp, excellent for consistent and modern UI conventions, but currently missing important features.

ArtCraft: I have not actually tried it, although it sounds very much like what you would expect from vibe coding: buggy as heck, feature deficient, and definitely not ready for serious consideration. Yet.

To be honest, I do most of my graphics work in Inkscape these days (lots of vector icon design). Brilliant UI, consistent UI conventions. Very usable. But mostly useless for photos.

I see plenty of posts from authors who didn't even bother trying any of these clones.

It seems it's buzzing because it make people who post about it, buzz.

We live a strange time.

I don't know. As others mentioned, Gimp and others had plenty of decades of oxygen to breathe. Meanwhile, the software ecosystem keeps getting worse - that's a trajectory it was on before LLMs, so AI is not to blame here.

I find such vibe-coded efforts to resonate with me, because they reflect the same impatience I have. Impatience with enshittification of the commercial offerings, impatience with OSS following suit without realizing it (most modern UI/UX philosophy is driven by needs of enshittification), impatience with OSS being dominated by fakers and itself becoming a business model. Impatience with broken software.

Vibe-coding can be a way to vent the frustration, and in this case, it even turns into a spectator sport. Most of the vibe-coded projects I do, and that I see people I know doing, share the same, single, deep motivation - "I want a software that does this particular thing right now, and without all the bullshit". The vibe is that of awe, but it starts rooted in anger.

children.text:
Rigorous specification doesn't even help, the rigority of a good spec requires too much context for LLMs to adhere to and they will flagrantly violate clear specifications once you have too much detail. The only thing that does work is having specification encoded as tests, because LLMs can fix compile errors in a loop and that deterministic guidance is what they need to keep them on track, but... writing tests is coding. Writing good tests still requires understanding the code and architecture in fine detail.

This is why you see all of these headlines about porting things that already have years of human work as deterministic guidelines and yet absolutely nothing worth using in production is being vibe coded from scratch. Don't let the hype/FOMO get to you, you are not alone, that is just what the people selling you the hype want you to believe.
